title: OpenAI expands free ChatGPT for researchers to 200,000 with 50,000 new grants
summary: If you do research and are hesitating about paying for ChatGPT: OpenAI is expanding free access for researchers to up to 200,000 worldwide, with 50,000 new grants available first come, first served from November 23.
ai_summary: OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers from July's small pilot into a free program for up to 200,000 researchers worldwide. The next round opens November 23 and will award 50,000 grants on a first come, first served basis; each grant covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 people this round. Two things change from the pilot: selection moves from a lottery to first come, first served, and the free tier moves from ChatGPT Pro to ChatGPT Plus, because OpenAI says usage data showed most participants stayed within Plus limits. By default, data shared through the program is not used to train models. It suits researchers who want to apply frontier models to their work without worrying about subscription costs; the announcement does not give the standard Plus price or detailed eligibility criteria.
brief: The next round opens 50,000 free grants on November 23, first come, first served—no more lottery.
Each grant covers the recipient plus up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers this round.
The free tier moves from ChatGPT Pro in the pilot to ChatGPT Plus; by default, data shared through the program is not used to train models.
The pilot has drawn 20,000 researchers across 33 countries; surveyed participants estimated the same work without AI would take nearly twice as long.

sections.h: What it is: OpenAI turns a pilot into a bigger free ChatGPT program for researchers

blocks.p: On November 16, 2026, OpenAI announced it is expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers. In short, the program gives eligible researchers free ChatGPT access so they can apply frontier models to their work rather than being kept out by subscription fees. It began as a small pilot in July and now moves into a larger round.

sections.h: How the new round works: first come, first served, one grant for you plus two collaborators

blocks.p: Applications open Monday, November 23. The biggest change from the pilot: no more lottery—selection is now first come, first served. The first 50,000 eligible applications will receive a grant. If you are already on the waitlist and qualify, OpenAI will email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

fig.title: Three rules changed between the pilot and this round
fig.subtitle: Amber marks this round's new changes; neutral marks the pilot approach; gray means the announcement doesn't specify.
fig.footer: First come, first served means: if you're eligible, applying earlier is safer—it's no longer down to luck.

blocks.p: Each grant gives the recipient free ChatGPT Plus access, plus up to two collaborators. So this round's ceiling is 150,000 people: 50,000 grants with up to two collaborators each.

fig.title: One grant can connect the recipient and up to two collaborators

fig.note: When all 50,000 grants include their full collaborators, they cover up to 150,000 researchers.

callout.title: 150,000 is a ceiling, not a guarantee
callout.text: The 150,000 figure only applies if every grant includes two collaborators; the actual number covered depends on how many people each grant includes.

sections.h: Why swap free ChatGPT Pro for Plus?

blocks.p: The pilot gave researchers ChatGPT Pro, the pricier tier with higher limits and compute. After reviewing pilot usage, OpenAI said most participants actually stayed within ChatGPT Plus limits, so Plus was enough. This round therefore offers ChatGPT Plus, freeing up capacity to cover more teams.

callout.title: Enough for most projects, but watch heavy compute
callout.text: If your research runs large computations for long periods, Plus limits may feel tighter than Pro. The announcement gives no specific limits for either tier, so a direct comparison isn't possible.

sections.h: Pilot results: 20,000 researchers across 33 countries, saving nearly half the time

blocks.p: Since the pilot launched in July, 20,000 researchers across 33 countries have joined. OpenAI's Economic Research team published a report, 'Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT', based on surveys of more than 1,800 pilot participants.
One striking figure: surveyed participants estimated that without AI, the same research at the same quality would take nearly twice as long.

callout.title: How to read 'nearly twice as long'
callout.text: It's a self-estimate from survey respondents, not a controlled experiment measurement, so read it with some caution.

sections.h: What do researchers actually do with ChatGPT?

blocks.p: The pilot includes two public examples: one in medicine and one in biodiversity.

fig.title: Pilot use cases: from drug targets to museum specimens
fig.subtitle: Cards are research cases mentioned in the announcement, plus one program-wide benefit.

items.title: Finding new drug targets
items.desc: Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School, is exploring whether ChatGPT can link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development; one goal is shorter tuberculosis treatment.

items.title: Turning specimen photos into databases
items.desc: Arthur Porto's team at the Florida Museum of Natural History uses AI to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also built a 3D butterfly model whose wings change color as you turn it.

items.title: Frontier models + training
items.desc: Participants can use OpenAI's frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research.

sections.h: Beyond this program, what other access do researchers have?

blocks.p: ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one route. OpenAI also offers ChatGPT Edu for university research, teaching, and learning, with data analysis tools and administrative controls; and GPT-Rosalind for biology research, combining specialized biological reasoning with access to scientific tools and databases.

blocks.p: The Rosalind Academic Plan gives eligible U.S. university labs up to 30 free seats for up to 12 months, but access to GPT-Rosalind requires approval through the trusted-access process.
In mathematics, OpenAI also contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

sections.h: Pricing and privacy: how free is it, and will your data be used for training?

blocks.p: On pricing: this round gives away ChatGPT Plus, and the 50,000 grants themselves are free. But the announcement doesn't state the standard ChatGPT Plus price or the ChatGPT Pro price from the pilot, so there is no way to calculate how much you save.
On privacy: by default, data shared through the program is not used to train models. Note the 'by default'—the announcement doesn't explain any exceptions.

list: The standard ChatGPT Plus subscription price, and the ChatGPT Pro price during the pilot: not stated in the announcement.
What 'eligible' actually requires: the announcement only says eligible, without listing criteria.
How long the 50,000 grants will take to be claimed, or how they will be allocated by country: not stated.
Whether pilot participants who received Pro will be automatically renewed or downgraded this round: not stated.
Application deadline: the announcement only says applications open November 23, with no closing date.
Whether there are exceptions or opt-ins beyond 'not trained by default': not stated.

blocks.p: The value is straightforward: eligible researchers, plus up to two collaborators, can use ChatGPT Plus for free on their projects, with training included, and by default OpenAI won't train on your data. The trade-off is that it only covers ChatGPT Plus, which may be insufficient for heavy compute, and you have to secure a grant first.

list: If your project involves lots of looking up sources, writing code, cleaning up data, and drafting papers, and your team is just you plus up to two collaborators, this round is worth applying for early.
If you're on the waitlist, check your inbox: eligible researchers will receive activation instructions before applications open.
If you're a U.S. university lab working in biology, also look at the Rosalind Academic Plan's 30 free seats.
If you need to run large batches of computation over long periods, check whether Plus limits are enough—the announcement gives no specific caps.
